Family Health

Wrinkled nipples and other texture changes: what to notice

Updated: October 5, 2026

Written and edited byMohammadamin Namyar, founder of BeMama: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

Nipples can look smooth at one moment and puckered at another. Cold, touch and feeding can change their appearance, while dryness, pregnancy and ageing may bring longer-lasting differences. A wrinkled appearance alone does not identify the cause. The useful distinction is between a familiar, temporary change and a new or persistent change, especially one accompanied by a rash, discharge, pain, a lump or inward pulling.

Why nipple shape and texture can change

Nipples contain openings through which milk can pass from the breast ducts. The surrounding darker area is the areola, which contains glands that produce oily secretions and help protect the skin. Small visible bumps in this area can be part of normal anatomy.

Muscle fibres in the nipple and areola respond to stimulation. Cold temperatures, touch or feeding can make the nipple more prominent and the surrounding skin look gathered or wrinkled. This can change again as the stimulus passes. Cold exposure here means temperature, not having a respiratory infection.

There is considerable normal variation. Nipples can project, lie relatively flat or point inward, and areolae vary in size and colour from pink to deep brown. Comparing your appearance with someone else’s photograph is less useful than noticing what is usual for you.

A temporary surface crease is not the same thing as a new, persistent indentation of the breast skin or a nipple that has recently become pulled inward. Those changes deserve assessment even if they initially look like ordinary wrinkling.

Dry skin and eczema

Dryness can make fine lines more noticeable. With eczema or another form of dermatitis, the area may also itch, become sore, flake or develop crusting. More active inflammation can cause small blisters, weeping or cracks. A rough surface can therefore look wrinkled without the underlying nipple shape having changed.

Possible triggers include soap, fragranced products, detergent residue, friction and ingredients in creams. An existing tendency to eczema may matter, but nipple or areolar dermatitis can also appear without a history of eczema elsewhere.

Keep track of new products and whether one or both sides are affected. Do not assume a persistent nipple rash is simply dry skin, particularly if it is on one side, involves the nipple itself, bleeds or does not improve with appropriate treatment. A clinician can distinguish dermatitis from infection and less common conditions.

Hormonal changes across life

Breast tissue responds to hormones during puberty, the menstrual cycle, pregnancy, lactation and menopause. Fullness, tenderness, nipple prominence and areolar colour can change. These changes may make skin folds appear different even when the skin itself is healthy.

Before a period, temporary swelling or tenderness can alter how the breast and nipple look. During pregnancy, breasts may enlarge and the areolae may become larger or darker as the body prepares for feeding. There is no single amount of enlargement that every person experiences.

Weight gain or loss can also alter breast volume and the way the skin lies over it. That is not proof of a hormone disorder. Notice whether a change settles with your usual cycle or persists, and do not explain away a new one-sided abnormality as hormonal without advice.

Ageing and breast shape

Over time, skin and supporting tissues become less elastic, and the proportions of glandular tissue and fat in the breast change. Menopause can contribute to these changes. Breasts may feel less firm or sit differently, and their size may increase or decrease rather than following one predictable pattern.

The skin around the nipple can look more folded as breast volume changes. Some changes are gradual and familiar. You do not need to reverse ordinary ageing or restore a previous shape for your breasts to be healthy.

However, a nipple newly turning inward should not automatically be attributed to age. The timing, whether one or both sides are affected, and any associated lump, discharge or skin change help a clinician decide what evaluation is needed.

Flat or inverted nipples

Some people have flat or inverted nipples from early life. An inverted nipple points inward, and folds around it may create a wrinkled appearance. If this has always been your pattern and there are no new symptoms, it may simply be an anatomical variation.

A nipple can become temporarily less prominent when the breast is very full or swollen. Longstanding inversion, short-lived changes with stimulation and newly acquired persistent inversion are different situations. Do not rely on stress or temperature as an explanation for a change that remains.

Flat or inverted nipples do not automatically prevent breastfeeding. Babies attach to a mouthful of breast tissue rather than only the nipple. A feeding professional can assess attachment and milk transfer and suggest support when needed.

New inversion, especially on one side, needs a clinical assessment. Benign conditions can cause it, but so can conditions that require treatment. Pulling or suctioning the nipple outward is not a way to rule out an underlying problem.

During pregnancy, breastfeeding and weaning

Pregnancy can change breast size, skin and nipple colour whether or not you breastfeed. During lactation, changes in fullness can make the nipple and areola look different before and after a feed. After weaning, breast volume may change again and the skin may sit more loosely.

Some people notice stretch marks, a different breast contour or a lasting change in areolar colour; others notice little difference. These variations do not measure how well breastfeeding went. Nor does everyone return to exactly the same breast size or nipple appearance they had before pregnancy.

The source of discomfort matters more than the presence of a crease. Persistent pain, cracks, bleeding or repeated distortion after feeds deserves support. Infection cannot be diagnosed simply from wrinkling, and a healthy-looking surface does not by itself show that the baby is transferring enough milk.

When feeding compresses or damages the nipple

A nipple that comes out of the baby’s mouth flattened, pinched, wedged or unusually white can suggest a shallow attachment. Friction and compression may also cause soreness or cracks. Ask a midwife or lactation professional to observe a full feed rather than trying to treat the appearance alone.

Changing positioning and attachment may help, but ongoing pain can have more than one cause. Mention colour changes, pain between feeds, a rash, discharge and any symptoms in the baby. Pump fit and technique are relevant if expression is uncomfortable.

Change breast pads when damp, use clean feeding equipment and handle irritated skin gently. Pat dry rather than rubbing. Repeated washing with soap, scrubbing or disinfecting after every feed can worsen dryness. If a cream or medicine is recommended, ask how to use it around feeding and whether residue needs to be removed.

If pain is preventing feeding or the baby’s intake is in doubt, ask promptly for a feeding and milk-expression plan. Improving comfort should go together with protecting the baby’s nutrition, not waiting for the nipple to look smooth.

Smoking, sunlight and other exposures

Smoking and ultraviolet exposure contribute to skin ageing in general. Exposed breast skin can be affected just like other skin. Irritating chemicals or repeated friction can also change the surface, although a nipple change cannot be traced to one exposure from appearance alone.

Covering the area with clothing is a practical way to limit sun exposure. Use appropriate sun protection on exposed skin. If breastfeeding, discuss any product applied directly where the baby’s mouth will touch; avoiding direct exposure and covering the breast can simplify this.

A label such as natural or chemical-free does not guarantee that a product is suitable for nipple skin or for contact with an infant’s mouth. Stop a product that causes irritation and seek advice about persistent symptoms.

Quitting smoking has benefits beyond the skin. If you want help, a clinician or stop-smoking service can discuss a plan that fits your circumstances, including pregnancy or breastfeeding. Wrinkles should not become another reason to blame yourself.

Breast changes that should not be treated as a cosmetic problem

Most breast changes are not cancer, but new changes should be checked. Examples include persistent inward pulling of a nipple, a lump, skin dimpling, a change in breast shape or discharge that is not breast milk. Spontaneous bloody or clear discharge from one nipple deserves particular attention.

Flaking, crusting, bleeding or a sore that does not heal also needs assessment. The important question is not whether the nipple looks wrinkled enough to be concerning. A subtle new change may still deserve attention, and a visibly folded nipple may be entirely normal for that person.

Breast cancer can occur in people of any sex who have breast tissue. Do not dismiss a symptom because it seems unlikely at your age or because you recently had a normal screening result. A clinician can decide whether examination, imaging or another test is appropriate.

Inflammatory breast cancer and rapid changes

Inflammatory breast cancer is an uncommon form of breast cancer that can cause rapid swelling, warmth, redness or darker discolouration. The skin may develop ridges or pits resembling orange peel, and the nipple may pull inward. There may be no distinct lump.

Pain, heaviness or burning can occur, but these symptoms can also have other causes, including mastitis or another infection. The appearance is not a diagnosis. Rapidly developing breast swelling or skin change needs prompt medical evaluation.

Do not wait for a routine screening appointment or repeatedly try moisturizers if the breast is becoming inflamed or changing quickly. If treatment for an assumed infection does not lead to the expected improvement, follow up so that the diagnosis can be reconsidered.

Paget disease of the breast can resemble eczema

Paget disease is a rare cancer-related condition affecting the nipple and sometimes the areola. It can produce a persistent eczema-like rash with flaking, redness, itching, burning or crusting. The nipple may become flattened, ulcerated or otherwise changed.

It is more often diagnosed in older adults, but age alone cannot exclude it, and it can affect men. A persistent one-sided nipple rash should not be treated indefinitely as eczema without a clinician reviewing the response.

A clinician may recommend a small skin sample, called a biopsy, if the appearance raises concern. Imaging may also be needed to examine the breast tissue. Most itchy or dry skin is not Paget disease, but a diagnosis requires more than comparing symptoms with an online picture.

Can the areola become wrinkled too?

Yes. The areola is skin surrounding the nipple and can show folds, dryness and changes in texture. Its glands and natural secretions are part of normal breast anatomy. Pregnancy, lactation, ageing, changes in breast volume and temporary muscle contraction can all affect its appearance.

The same distinctions apply as for the nipple: longstanding or temporary variation is different from persistent new rash, crusting, dimpling or another focal change. Areolar colour and texture vary widely, so assess a change against your own usual appearance.

Avoid squeezing the small areolar glands or trying to scrub the surface smooth. If there is a painful bump, spreading inflammation, discharge or an area that will not heal, seek advice rather than assuming it is an ordinary gland or fold.

Moisturizers and wrinkle remedies: what they can and cannot do

For uncomplicated dryness, a bland, fragrance-free emollient may make the skin more comfortable. Treating confirmed eczema or another condition can also improve the surface. These steps do not necessarily erase normal folds or change nipple anatomy.

Aloe vera, lanolin and vitamin C products are often promoted for skin appearance. Research about facial wrinkles or general collagen changes does not establish that they safely reverse nipple wrinkles. A small or older facial study is not a reason to apply a cosmetic active ingredient to irritated nipple skin.

Lanolin may suit some people but can cause contact allergy in others. Botanicals, fragrances and preservatives can also irritate or sensitize the skin. More products are not necessarily better, particularly while breastfeeding. Check suitability with a clinician or pharmacist and stop anything that worsens the reaction.

Do not use a cosmetic cream to cover up a persistent rash, a bleeding area or new inversion. Home care is most useful after considering the cause, not as a substitute for investigating a new symptom.

Food, activity and claims about balancing hormones

A varied diet with adequate protein, healthy fats, fibre, fruit and vegetables supports general health. Regular activity, sleep and ways to manage stress may also help wellbeing. These habits are worthwhile without promising a particular nipple appearance.

They have not been established as a treatment that balances hormones to remove nipple wrinkles. Avoiding every simple carbohydrate, drinking green tea or adding antioxidant-rich foods does not diagnose or correct a hormone disorder. Associations between diet and facial skin appearance cannot establish a nipple treatment.

Choose realistic habits rather than a restrictive wrinkle-prevention diet. If a hormonal problem is suspected because of a wider set of symptoms, discuss it with a clinician. The right assessment is more useful than supplements marketed as hormone balancers.

Nipple stretching, suction devices and surgery

You may encounter advice about the Hoffman technique, manual stimulation, syringe-based suction or commercial nipple correctors. These approaches concern nipple projection, not the treatment of ordinary surface wrinkles. Their usefulness depends on the situation, and they should not be used to postpone assessment of new inversion.

If feeding is difficult, ask a lactation professional to demonstrate any appropriate technique and check the baby’s intake. Do not improvise forceful stretching or suction, especially on cracked, painful or inflamed skin. A deeper attachment or another feeding adjustment may be more relevant than making the nipple protrude.

Surgery is sometimes considered for persistent inversion after assessment and discussion of the person’s goals. Techniques differ in how they handle the milk ducts. Possible effects include altered sensation, scarring, recurrence and difficulty breastfeeding afterward; preserving ducts does not guarantee future lactation.

A stable nipple shape does not require cosmetic correction. If you want to explore treatment, ask about the expected benefit, recovery, risks and implications for future feeding before deciding.

When to book an assessment and how screening fits

Book an appointment for a new or persistent nipple or breast change, especially one-sided inversion, non-milk discharge, a lump, a rash that does not settle or skin dimpling. Seek prompt help for a rapidly red, hot, swollen or painful breast, particularly with fever or feeling unwell.

Tell the clinician when the change began, whether it comes and goes, how it relates to feeding or the menstrual cycle and which products you have tried. A photograph of a temporary change may help describe it, but taking one should not delay needed care.

Routine breast screening is for people without symptoms and follows local age and risk guidance. Symptom assessment is separate. There is no universal instruction that everyone starts the same mammogram schedule at 40, and a new concern should not wait until you reach a screening age.

Knowing your usual breast or chest appearance can help you notice changes. It is not a guarantee of early cancer detection and does not replace recommended screening. The aim is informed attention without repeatedly checking or treating every normal crease as disease.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

NCI and NHS guidance recommend assessment of new nipple or breast changes even after a recent normal screening result. Persistent nipple rash, new inversion and rapid inflammatory changes should not be managed only as wrinkles.

Dermatology and infant-feeding guidance support finding the cause of irritation and correcting painful attachment. Facial anti-wrinkle evidence does not establish an effective nipple treatment.

How BeMama can help

Use care notes to record when a change started, associated symptoms and questions for an appointment. Keep personal photographs private and share them only if you choose and your clinician has an appropriate channel.

When to seek help

Seek prompt care for a rapidly changing, hot or swollen breast, fever or feeling unwell. Arrange assessment of a new lump, inversion, non-milk discharge or persistent one-sided nipple rash.

Evidence notes updated: October 5, 2026

Key takeaways

  • Temporary nipple puckering can be normal.
  • Dryness, hormonal changes, breast volume and feeding can affect texture.
  • New inversion or persistent rash needs assessment rather than cosmetic treatment.
  • Wrinkle creams and hormone-balancing diets are not established nipple treatments.
  • Painful feeding deserves an attachment and milk-transfer review.
  • Symptoms should be assessed separately from routine breast screening.

Frequently asked questions

Is it normal for a nipple to look wrinkled when I am cold?

Temporary puckering can occur as muscle fibres respond to cold or touch. A new change that remains or comes with other symptoms should be checked.

Can I assume new nipple inversion is just ageing?

No. Age-related changes can occur, but new persistent inversion deserves assessment, especially on one side.

Does a wrinkled nipple mean breast cancer?

Not by itself. Many changes are benign. A new lump, inward pulling, discharge, dimpling or persistent rash needs clinical review.

Can a flat or inverted nipple still work for breastfeeding?

Often, yes. Attachment involves breast tissue as well as the nipple. A feeding professional can help assess comfort and milk transfer.

Why is my nipple pinched or flattened after feeding?

Shallow attachment can compress it. Ask for an observed feed, particularly if there is pain, cracking or concern about the baby’s intake.

Should I use aloe vera or vitamin C to remove nipple wrinkles?

They are not established treatments for this purpose and may irritate the area. Evidence about facial wrinkles does not establish nipple safety or benefit.

Is lanolin always safe for irritated skin?

No. Some people develop contact allergy. Ask about a suitable product and stop one that worsens symptoms.

Will diet or green tea balance hormones and smooth the nipple?

No such treatment effect is established. General healthy habits can support wellbeing without changing normal nipple anatomy.

Should I use a suction device for a newly inverted nipple?

Have the new change assessed first. For feeding problems, use techniques or devices only with appropriate guidance rather than forceful DIY suction.

Can I wait for my next screening mammogram?

A new symptom needs its own assessment, even after a recent normal mammogram. Routine screening and symptom investigation serve different purposes.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
